name: Op Art Moire
basis: two line gratings, one bent by the picture, beating into moire (how)

lumenary.blurb: Two sets of fine lines, one of them bent by your picture. Where they cross, beats appear that were never drawn.

facts.bestOn: Bold shapes and portraits with simple tones

why: When two fine patterns of lines overlap, broad bands appear that are in neither of them. These are beats, the visual cousin of two close musical notes giving a slow throb. Op artists realised that these illusions seem to shimmer and move, and that a small change in the lines makes a large change in the bands, so the picture bends one set of lines and the beats follow its shapes.
how: Draw one plain set of lines, rings or waves with a fixed period.
Draw a second set with the same period, turned a little or with a shifted centre.
Shift the coordinate across the second set by up to 9 periods times the picture’s lightness minus a half, so the lines swerve around shapes.
Set the thickness of the second set from the picture’s tone, mixing the duty cycle between a half and a value that follows darkness.
The beats are not drawn at all: they appear where the two sets cross, and for equal period at an angle α they are p / (2 sin(α/2)) apart.
history: The word moiré is French and refers to watered silk, in which two layers of cloth make shimmering patterns. Op art, as a name, appeared in Time magazine in 1964, and the exhibition The Responsive Eye at the Museum of Modern Art in New York in 1965 made artists such as Bridget Riley and Victor Vasarely famous. Engineers also use moiré fringes to measure tiny strains and displacements.
uses: Detecting strain and deformation in engineering
Avoiding unwanted screen patterns in printing and photography
terms: A pattern that appears when two regular patterns overlap.
A slow variation that arises when two close frequencies are combined.
The share of each period that is filled with ink.
paragraphs: When two sets of fine regular lines overlap, broad dark and light bands appear that are in neither set. They are the beats of the two patterns, the same effect as two close musical notes giving a slow throb. The program draws two sets. The first is a plain set of parallel lines (or rings, or gentle waves) of period p. The second has the same period but is turned by the angle slider, or has its centre shifted for rings. For two sets of equal period at an angle α the bands are p / (2 sin(α/2)) apart, so a small turn makes wide, dramatic fringes.

The picture enters in two ways. First it bends the second set: the coordinate across its lines is shifted by up to 9 periods times (L − ½), where L is the lightness, so the lines swerve around shapes and the beats trace them. Second, it sets the weight: the duty cycle of the second set is mixed between ½ and 0.12 + 0.76 (1 − L), so lines are thick in the dark and thin in the light. Each stripe is anti-aliased with a smoothstep one pixel wide, and the two sets combine as ink coverage, as if printed one over the other.

equations.note: Spacing of the moiré bands for equal periods p and a relative turn α.
The picture bends the second set: u₂ is the coordinate across its lines, in periods.
Ink coverage of the union; dist(u) = |u − ⌊u⌋ − ½| is the distance to the nearest stripe centre, a = 0.8 px / period the anti-alias width, δ the duty cycle.

presets.text: Concentric rings give the classic target fringes.
A bigger turn of the second grid packs the bands closer.
Strong warp lets the picture appear in the bending lines.
